title: Psilocybin’s lasting action requires pyramidal cell types and 5-HT2A receptors
summary: In mouse medial frontal cortex, one dose of psilocybin grew dendritic spines on both pyramidal-tract (subcortical-projecting) and intratelencephalic neurons, but only the pyramidal-tract cells mattered for behaviour: silencing them abolished psilocybin's anti-stress effects, and only they showed boosted synaptic calcium signals and firing acutely. Knocking out 5-HT2A receptors in this region wiped out both the plasticity and the behavioural benefit.
caveats: Mouse-only, with stress-related behaviours as a stand-in for depression; one brain region and cell-type silencing rather than human data. Strong mechanistic evidence that 5-HT2A matters for the lasting effects in mice, but doesn't settle whether the trip itself is needed in humans.
